entries.title: Old money
entries.gist: Old wealth is quiet and slightly worn: things are inherited, repaired, used for decades. Status shows in access and ease (who they can call, what they never have to ask), not in labels.
entries.avoid: logos, gold everywhere, talk about prices, a butler named Jeeves
pool: a cashmere sweater with a darned elbow
a signet ring worn smooth
a car twenty years old and perfectly kept
an umbrella stand of walking sticks nobody uses
a family portrait hung slightly crooked and never fixed
a club membership that comes with a waiting list of decades
thank-you letters on engraved card
a cold house because heating the east wing is 'absurd'
summers at the same place since childhood
knowing which fork without thinking, and not caring who doesn't
a dog more important than most guests
a tailor who has their measurements since school

entries.title: New money and status display
entries.gist: New wealth is visible and time-starved: assistants, schedules, things bought for the experience or the photo. The anxiety is about access and being taken seriously by older money.
entries.avoid: the word 'expensive' in every line, champagne in every scene, a character who only talks about money
pool: a phone that never stops buzzing, answered by an assistant
a watch on a waitlist bought through a 'friend of the dealer'
a chef hired for one dinner
a penthouse with almost no furniture and perfect lighting
a driver who also handles the security briefing
art bought on an advisor's word
a private jet that is really a share in a fleet
a membership to a members-only club in three cities
the same sneakers in six colours
a wellness routine with a cold plunge at 5 a.m.
renting the whole restaurant rather than waiting for a table

entries.title: Jewellery and fine objects
entries.gist: Fine jewellery has weight, temperature and history: clasps, settings, repairs, who wore it before. Describe one specific piece by how it behaves, not by its value.
entries.avoid: 'glittering diamonds', 'priceless necklace', jewels described only by price
pool: a pearl strand that has to be restrung every few years
a brooch pinned on the left because 'that is where it goes'
earrings heavy enough to leave a mark by evening
a ring resized twice for different hands
an Art Deco clasp that needs two hands
a locket with a photo nobody remembers
a chain warm from being worn all day
a stone with a small inclusion only the owner knows is there
a pair of cufflinks borrowed and never returned
a tiara kept in a bank vault, worn once a decade

entries.title: Regency and early 19th-century dress
entries.gist: Regency clothing is light muslin for women, layered tailoring for men; dressing takes help and time, and clothes signal rank, mourning, marriage status.
entries.avoid: corsets cinched to fainting, everyone in silk ballgowns all day
pool: a high-waisted muslin dress that shows every grass stain
a spencer jacket against the evening chill
kid gloves removed only to eat
a reticule too small for anything but a fan and a card
a cravat tied in a style with its own name
Hessian boots polished by someone else
a shawl that is half the point of the outfit
half-mourning grey and lavender
a bonnet brim that hides the face from the side
ink-stained cuffs on a man who writes his own letters

entries.title: Victorian dress
entries.gist: Victorian clothes are heavy, layered and rule-bound: different outfits for morning, visiting, dinner and mourning; dark wool and soot in the city.
entries.avoid: every woman in a huge ballgown, corsets as torture devices in every scene
pool: a bustle that makes sitting a negotiation
jet beads for mourning
a high collar with a cameo at the throat
mud-stained hems from city streets
a gentleman's watch chain across the waistcoat
detachable celluloid collars
a walking dress for the park, different from the visiting dress
button boots needing a buttonhook
a governess in dark grey with no ornament
gloves for every occasion, a different length for each

entries.title: 1920s fashion
entries.gist: The 1920s cut hair and hems: straight dropped-waist dresses, bobbed hair, cloche hats; men in wider trousers and boaters in summer. Movement and dancing shaped the clothes.
entries.avoid: every scene a Gatsby party with champagne towers and feathers
pool: a beaded dress heavy enough to swing when she turns
a cloche hat pulled down to the eyebrows
rolled stockings and rouged knees
a long string of pearls knotted at the chest
two-tone spectator shoes
a raccoon coat at a college game
Oxford bags, trousers wide as skirts
a cigarette holder that is mostly a prop
a dropped waist that makes curves irrelevant
a fresh bob that still feels strange on the neck

entries.title: Streetwear and contemporary casual
entries.gist: Contemporary casual is about fit, brand signals and small choices: how the hoodie hangs, which sneakers, what is clean and what is deliberately worn.
entries.avoid: 'casual jeans and a t-shirt' for everyone, or every character in designer labels
pool: sneakers kept in their box between wears
a hoodie two sizes up, sleeves over the hands
cargo pants with every pocket empty
a thrifted band tee for a band they've never heard
a crossbody bag worn at the chest
socks pulled up over track pants
a puffer jacket on in a warm café
a silver chain that keeps catching on the collar
headphones around the neck all day, never on
a cap worn backwards only indoors

entries.title: Goth and alternative fashion
entries.gist: Alternative fashion is a craft and a community: DIY, layered black textures, deliberate choices, and a history (post-punk, trad goth, emo, grunge) people care about.
entries.avoid: goths as sad and edgy, 'dressed in black' as the whole description
pool: a jacket covered in hand-sewn patches
platform boots that add four inches and take ten minutes to lace
fishnets under ripped jeans
silver rings on every finger, one from a grandmother
black lipstick worn off on a coffee cup
a velvet coat from a charity shop
safety pins holding a hem that tore years ago
eyeliner that took twenty minutes and looks effortless
a band shirt from an actual gig in 2009
studded belt, one stud missing

entries.title: Office and corporate dress
entries.gist: Office clothes signal rank quietly: fit, fabric, what you are allowed to skip. The higher up, the more casual you are permitted to be.
entries.avoid: 'a sharp suit' for every powerful man, a pencil skirt for every woman
pool: a lanyard tucked into the shirt pocket
a blazer left on the chair to look present
trainers under the desk, heels in the bag
a quarter-zip fleece with a company logo
a tie loosened after six
a suit that fits at the shoulders and nowhere else
a coffee stain hidden under a buttoned jacket
reading glasses pushed into the hair
a CEO in a plain grey t-shirt that costs more than the intern's suit
a security badge that has to be tapped twice

entries.title: Military and service uniforms
entries.gist: Uniforms carry rules: rank insignia, how they are worn, what is out of regulation. Field and dress uniforms are different worlds.
entries.avoid: uniforms that are always crisp, medals clanking in every scene
pool: boots broken in over months
a sleeve rolled to the regulation fold
a cap carried under the arm indoors
name tape faded from washing
a unit patch they are quietly proud of
a dress uniform kept in a garment bag for funerals and weddings
dog tags taped so they don't clink
a lanyard of keys only a quartermaster carries
creases ironed with a ruler
a field jacket with a pen in every pocket

entries.title: Ukrainian food
entries.gist: Ukrainian home food is seasonal, generous and regional: soups, dough, preserves, the dacha harvest. Who cooked it and whose recipe matters more than the dish.
entries.avoid: borscht in every scene, 'hearty peasant food'
pool: green borscht with sorrel and a halved egg
varenyky with sour cherries and sugar in summer
garlic pampushky still warm
deruny with sour cream at a dacha
a jar of grandmother's pickles opened for guests
uzvar of dried fruit at Christmas Eve
kutia with poppy seed and honey
banosh with brynza in the Carpathians
salo sliced thin on black bread with garlic
holubtsi rolled the night before
kvas from a street barrel in summer
syrnyky for breakfast, slightly burnt on one side

entries.title: Japanese food
entries.gist: Japanese food culture runs from convenience-store onigiri to izakaya to formal kaiseki; seasonality and small rituals (oshibori, itadakimasu) matter.
entries.avoid: sushi as the only Japanese food
pool: convenience-store onigiri with the clever wrapper
a late-night ramen counter with a ticket machine
an oshibori towel steaming on arrival
yakitori and cheap beer at an izakaya
a bento with a carrot cut like a flower
natto that divides the table
a kaiseki course too beautiful to start
takoyaki burning the roof of the mouth
a can of hot coffee from a vending machine in winter
matcha whisked badly by a beginner

entries.title: Italian food
entries.gist: Italian food is regional and rule-bound: no cappuccino after a meal, the right pasta shape for the sauce, Sunday lunches that last hours.
entries.avoid: spaghetti and meatballs, everyone shouting 'mamma mia'
pool: an espresso drunk standing at the bar in two sips
cacio e pepe that seizes if the water is wrong
a nonna's ragù that takes all Sunday
aperitivo with olives and crisps
a trattoria with no menu, only what the owner decided
fresh pasta drying on a broom handle
a bitter amaro after dinner
a risotto stirred for exactly as long as it takes
a cappuccino ordered at 4 p.m. and the waiter's look
panettone arguments at Christmas

entries.title: French food and café culture
entries.gist: French food culture is ritual and time: the morning baguette run, the long lunch, the apéro, the cheese course; bistros, brasseries and patisseries are different places.
entries.avoid: snooty waiters and snails in every scene
pool: a baguette carried home with the end already eaten
a croissant flaking all over a dark coat
an apéro with saucisson cut on a board
a cheese course before dessert, never after
a café crème lasting an hour at a terrace table
a steak ordered 'bleu'
a patisserie box tied with ribbon
a Sunday market with a cheese seller who argues about ripeness
a bottle of house red in a carafe
a tarte tatin flipped badly at home

entries.title: Levantine and Middle Eastern food
entries.gist: Levantine food is shared: mezze tables, bread as cutlery, mint tea or coffee with cardamom, hospitality that is hard to refuse.
entries.avoid: 'exotic spices' as the whole description
pool: a mezze table where nobody has their own plate
flatbread torn to scoop hummus
coffee with cardamom in a small cup, refilled before it's empty
fresh mint tea too sweet to finish
za'atar on bread for breakfast
fattoush with crisp fried bread
a shawarma stand with a queue at 2 a.m.
knafeh still hot with stretching cheese
pickled turnips bright pink
being told to eat more three times

entries.title: Chinese food by region
entries.gist: Chinese cooking is many cuisines: Sichuan heat, Cantonese dim sum, northern dumplings and noodles; meals are shared, and ordering is an art.
entries.avoid: takeout boxes and fortune cookies
pool: Sichuan peppercorn numbing the lips
dim sum trolleys and stamping the card
dumplings folded by the whole family at New Year
a bubbling hotpot split in two, spicy and mild
hand-pulled noodles slapped on the counter
jasmine tea refilled by tapping two fingers
a lazy Susan turning to the eldest first
xiaolongbao that burn if bitten too soon
breakfast youtiao dipped in soy milk
mooncakes given and regifted

entries.title: Street and late-night food
entries.gist: Street food is about the place and the hour: queues, steam, eating standing up, the vendor who knows regulars.
entries.avoid: 'greasy food' as the whole description
pool: a paper cone of chips with too much vinegar
a night market skewer eaten while walking
a kebab after the club, sauce on the sleeve
a food truck with a two-item menu and a queue
a vendor who starts the order before you speak
steam rising from a corn cart in winter
a hot dog with fried onions at a football ground
street tacos with lime and a radish
a paper plate folding under the weight
the one vendor still open at 4 a.m.

entries.title: Coffee and tea culture
entries.gist: Coffee and tea are rituals with tribes: specialty cafés, the office machine, a grandmother's samovar, a tea ceremony. How someone takes theirs says a lot.
entries.avoid: 'a steaming cup of coffee' in every morning scene
pool: a flat white with oat milk ordered without looking up
cold brew in a mason jar
instant coffee in a chipped mug at a night shift
a samovar at a dacha with jam on the side
a moka pot hissing on a gas ring
a tea bag left in too long on purpose
a pour-over that takes four minutes and a scale
a vending-machine coffee that tastes of plastic
builder's tea, strong, two sugars
a matcha latte photographed before drinking

entries.title: Laboratory work
entries.gist: Real lab work is slow, procedural and full of waiting: protocols, incubations, contamination, failed runs, booking equipment, and a lab notebook that has to be readable.
entries.avoid: 'the experiment was a success' after one try; every scientist a genius with a cold voice
pool: a centrifuge that walks across the bench when unbalanced
gloves changed every time the phone rings
a protocol annotated in three people's handwriting
a -80 freezer alarm at 3 a.m.
an overnight incubation that dictates the whole weekend
a contaminated plate and a week lost
booking the confocal microscope a month ahead
a fume hood sash pulled down to the line
coffee forbidden in the lab and drunk in the corridor
labels written on tape with a marker that's dying
a reviewer's comment quoted bitterly at lunch

entries.title: Hospitals and medicine
entries.gist: Hospital work is shifts, handovers and hierarchy; nurses run the ward, residents are exhausted, and most of the job is documentation, not heroics.
entries.avoid: a surgeon shouting 'clear!' over every patient, doctors with nothing to do but brood
pool: a handover at 7 a.m. with cold coffee
a pager going off mid-sentence
a nurse who knows the patient better than the consultant
scrubs that never quite fit
a resident asleep sitting up in the staff room
a whiteboard of beds in three colours of marker
hand gel on every doorframe
a family waiting in the corridor for the same news for hours
a consultant's ward round with students trailing
notes typed with one finger at the end of a 12-hour shift

entries.title: Astronomy and observatories
entries.gist: Modern astronomy is mostly data, code and night shifts at remote sites; observing time is competed for, and weather decides everything.
entries.avoid: a lone genius peering through a brass telescope every night
pool: a night of observing time lost to clouds
a control room warmer than the dome
a red flashlight to keep night vision
data reduction that takes months
the altitude headache at a mountain observatory
a telescope proposal rejected by one point
a light-pollution map on the wall
an amateur who spots the comet first

entries.title: Royal courts and nobility
entries.gist: Court life is etiquette, access and patronage: who stands where, who is received, who has the monarch's ear; power moves through favours, marriages and offices more than swords.
entries.avoid: a cartoonishly evil advisor, a king who decides everything by shouting
pool: a seating plan argued over for a week
the right to sit in the queen's presence
a lady-in-waiting who hears everything
petitions read by a secretary first
a marriage negotiated through three ambassadors
a household office (Master of the Horse) worth more than land
a fall from favour signalled by an unreturned greeting
a progress through the provinces that ruins the hosts
precedence disputes at a funeral
a dowry paid in installments, the last one late

entries.title: Parliaments, elections and campaigns
entries.gist: Modern politics runs on coalitions, staff and timing: votes counted in advance, press cycles, donors, constituency work; the speech is the end of a long process.
entries.avoid: every politician a liar, one dramatic speech that changes everything
pool: a whip counting votes the night before
a committee hearing nobody watches
a staffer drafting the statement before the event happens
a constituency surgery about potholes
a leak timed for the Friday news cycle
a donor dinner with a seating chart
a coalition deal hinging on one ministry
a campaign bus with bad coffee
polling numbers read like weather
a vote missed because of a train delay

entries.title: Bureaucracy and offices
entries.gist: Bureaucracy is people following procedures: forms, stamps, queues, the clerk who can help or not. The drama is in exceptions, connections and deadlines.
entries.avoid: faceless evil bureaucrats
pool: a stamp that can only be given on Tuesdays
a queue number called out of order
a form that needs another form to be filled
a clerk who quietly tells you the shortcut
a document valid for three months that takes four to get
a photocopy of a photocopy
the right person on holiday
a box of chocolates to say thank you

entries.title: Organised crime
entries.gist: Organised crime is a business with family, loyalty and fear; most of it is logistics, money laundering and relationships with legitimate people, not shootouts.
entries.avoid: a sexy mafia boss who only says 'you're mine', constant shootouts
pool: a restaurant that is never busy and always open
an accountant more feared than the enforcers
a christening attended by people who shouldn't be seen together
a debt forgiven publicly and collected privately
a phone used once and thrown away
a cousin who runs the legal side
an unspoken rule about family at funerals
a favour that will be asked for in ten years
a meeting in a car with the radio on

entries.title: Vampires
entries.gist: Vampire lore varies by story: what sunlight does, invitations, reflections, how turning works, whether they need to sleep. Pick the rules this story uses and keep them; the best vampire stories are about time, hunger and what they lost.
entries.avoid: brooding in every scene, 'the hunger' as the only feeling, a velvet-and-candles castle by default
pool: old habits from their century (cash only, letter-writing)
a careful relationship with a blood supplier
a home with no mirrors and very good locks
slowness about the modern world, or obsessive keeping up
the need to be invited, played as etiquette
outliving every friend
a feeding that's clinical, not sensual
a sire who still writes once a decade
real fear of fire more than of stakes
a day-sleeper's blackout curtains held with tape

entries.title: Werewolves and shapeshifters
entries.gist: Shifter stories run on body and community: how changing feels, what the pack expects, control and its loss. Decide whether the moon forces it.
entries.avoid: 'alpha' as a personality, growling instead of talking
pool: clothes stashed in the woods for afterwards
an appetite nobody at the office understands
a pack meeting in someone's kitchen
scars that healed too fast to explain
a full moon schedule on the fridge
a sense of smell that makes cities exhausting
an elder who remembers the old territory lines
torn trainers, always

entries.title: The fae and fairy courts
entries.gist: Fae are bound by rules, not morality: they cannot lie but twist the truth; names, thanks, gifts and iron matter; bargains are literal. Their courts are beautiful and dangerous.
entries.avoid: pretty elves with no rules, 'mischievous' as their only trait
pool: never saying 'thank you' because it implies a debt
food in Faerie that keeps you there
a true name guarded like a password
iron nails in a doorframe
a bargain worded so the loophole is obvious only later
time passing differently: a night that was seven years
salt lines on a windowsill
a gift that cannot be refused politely

entries.title: Dragons
entries.gist: Dragons work best with a clear ecology and mind: how they fly, eat, think, what a hoard means to them, how long they live and remember.
entries.avoid: a dragon that is just a big angry lizard or just a sexy man with wings
pool: a hoard that is books or bells rather than gold
the smell of sulphur and warm stone
a dragon who counts its coins by sound
a rider's saddle scarred by heat
centuries-long grudges with specific names
molting scales sold on a black market
a lair heated like a sauna
a dragon who speaks slowly because humans are fast

entries.title: Magic schools and witchcraft
entries.gist: Magic schools are schools first: timetables, exams, houses or cliques, teachers with favourites, the cost of magic. Spells feel better when they have rules and price.
entries.avoid: Hogwarts copies, magic with no cost
pool: a spell that only works if you mean it
a familiar who judges your homework
an exam set in a room that moves
chalk circles scuffed by careless boots
a library section that requires a permission slip
herbs drying upside down in the dorm
a teacher who lost a hand to a mistake
a coven meeting that is mostly gossip and tea

entries.title: Demons and contracts
entries.gist: Demon stories turn on terms: what was asked, what was promised, the fine print. Demons are often bureaucratic, patient and very literal.
entries.avoid: a demon who only smirks and says 'mortal'
pool: a contract signed in something other than ink
a summoning circle with one smudged line
a demon who keeps immaculate records
a loophole the human found first
a name that cannot be spoken aloud
salt and iron that only slow them down
a deal for seven years exactly
hell's middle management, overworked

entries.title: Cultivation and xianxia
entries.gist: Cultivation stories have realms of power, sects with politics, face and debts of gratitude, and long seclusions. Progress is slow and costs resources and relationships.
entries.avoid: instant power-ups, every elder a villain
pool: a breakthrough attempted in seclusion for months
spirit stones counted like rent
a sect elder protecting their own disciple's face
a pill that has to be refined for days
a debt of gratitude repaid generations later
a junior who addresses everyone with the right title
a mountain gate with a thousand steps
a jade slip holding a technique

entries.title: Isekai and transported heroes
entries.gist: Transported-world stories are best about adjustment: language, food, missing home, what modern knowledge is useless, and what the locals think of the newcomer.
entries.avoid: an overpowered hero who knows everything, game menus in every line
pool: missing a specific snack from home
trying to explain a phone to someone
modern germ theory ignored by the local healer
a calendar that doesn't line up
learning to ride and being terrible at it
a word that means something rude here
keeping the clothes they arrived in
locals who've seen summoned heroes before and are tired of them

entries.title: Soulmates and fated bonds
entries.gist: Fated-bond stories are strongest when the bond creates problems: choice versus fate, the wrong timing, a bond that feels things the other hides.
entries.avoid: the bond solving every conflict instantly
pool: a soulmark that appears at the worst moment
feeling the other's pain across a city
a red thread only some can see
resenting the bond while wanting the person
a timer counting down to the meeting
a bond that broke once before
a family that arranged things around the fate
the first words written on the skin

entries.title: Omegaverse
entries.gist: Omegaverse is a fandom worldbuilding with a secondary dynamic (alpha, beta, omega) and its own biology: scent, heats and ruts, nesting, bonding marks, suppressants. Stories differ a lot in how society treats it; decide whether this world is hierarchical, modern and regulated, or somewhere between, and keep it consistent.
entries.avoid: alphas as only dominant and omegas as only submissive, everything reduced to scent and possessiveness
pool: scent blockers and suppressants with side effects
a scent described specifically (rain on asphalt, bitter orange), not just 'sweet'
a nest built from borrowed sweaters
heat leave written into labour law
a bonding mark that is a legal matter
a beta who's tired of being overlooked
scent-neutral public spaces
a doctor's note about cycle timing
